title: Major mergers
caption: The galaxy cluster SDSS J1336-0331, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: 6dFGS gJ133600.1-033130, SDSS J1336-0331 · constellation Virgo · about z=0.176 (redshift) away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The distortions across this image look like the work of a faulty lens, but they are real. The bright object at the centre is the galaxy cluster SDSS J1336-0331, and its enormous gravity warps the spacetime around it. This strong gravitational lensing bends the light of galaxies behind the cluster into arcs, which helps astronomers study those distant galaxies.

The cluster is interesting in its own right. It was part of a study of star formation in 42 Brightest Cluster Galaxies, or BCGs, the brightest galaxies in their clusters. BCGs usually sit at the centres of their clusters and rank among the Universe's most massive and luminous galaxies. Most are huge ellipticals and are likely to host active galactic nuclei.

The study found evidence that BCGs are fuelled by cold gas. In older BCGs, star formation no longer adds much to their growth, which comes instead through mergers. Violent, gas-rich mergers can trigger intense bursts of star formation.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed the cluster in visible and near-infrared light, from 390 nm to 1.6 μm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Much of this light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can.
